analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new oil and gas drilling leases off California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently prohibit new oil and gas leasing off California's coast was referred to committee in January 2021, never received a House vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban on new oil and gas leasing into the law governing the outer Continental Shelf, covering all federal waters off California's coast. It would stop any future sale of drilling rights there, while leaving existing leases and their holders' rights untouched. It never moved past its first committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: California coastal communities, beachgoers, and the tourism, fishing, and recreation economies that depend on clean water and unspoiled coastline. They would be permanently shielded from the spill risk and onshore industrial development that come with new offshore drilling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: California's coastal communities and tourism economy

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits oil and gas preleasing, leasing, and related activities in all outer Continental Shelf areas off California, overriding any other law that would allow it.
Makes the protection permanent by amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act directly, so it cannot be undone by a future administration's leasing plan.
Grandfathers rights under leases issued before enactment, so the ban targets only new drilling expansion, not existing operations.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would lose access to any new leasing off California. The federal Treasury would also forgo potential bonus bid, rent, and royalty revenue from leases that are never sold.

drawbacks.text: The ban forecloses domestic energy production and the federal royalty revenue that leasing off California could have generated, a cost its opponents would weigh against the environmental benefit.

Because existing leases are grandfathered, the bill does not shut down drilling that is already underway; it only prevents future expansion, so its effect depends on how much new leasing would otherwise have occurred.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a permanent, statutory shield against new offshore drilling off California, protecting a coast that drives large tourism and fishing economies from spill risk. The cost is forgone potential energy production and federal leasing revenue. Because the bill grandfathers existing leases, its practical effect is limited to blocking future expansion, making the environmental gain broad but the economic cost narrow.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the California Clean Coast Act on January 25, 2021, joined by 24 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced.
On February 18, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted 28 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee markup or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off: because no ban became law, new leasing off California remained legally possible under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and nothing changed. Coastal communities gained nothing beyond the protections already in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drilling interests, since nothing changed

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently prohibit oil and gas leasing off California's coast.

for.name: 28 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill then went to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee and no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 supporters in the House — the sponsor and 28 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor joined; the bill never reached a roll call, so no recorded partisan vote exists.

industries.note: The bill would permanently close new federal leasing off California to the industry, while grandfathering its existing leases. New drilling carries spill risk that falls on coastal residents and businesses, so the industry's interest in future expansion runs against the coast's.

industries.industry: California coastal tourism, fishing, and recreation
industries.note: A permanent leasing ban protects the clean beaches, fisheries, and coastline these businesses depend on, aligning their interest with coastal residents' desire to avoid new drilling and spill risk.
